title: How the Frick Fracking Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain hydraulic fracturing ("fracking") for natural gas and oil in shale rock: how horizontal wells are drilled, cemented, perforated with explosive charges, and pressurized with water, sand and chemicals. They cover the Marcellus Shale, the pro-fracking case (jobs, tax revenue, cleaner-burning natural gas, reduced foreign oil dependence) and the concerns (methane leaks, wastewater disposal, earthquakes, water use in drought areas, undisclosed chemicals, diesel use, and the 2005 Energy Policy Act exemption known as the "Halliburton loophole"). They also discuss industry-funded research controversies, notable accidents, and a new propane-gel fracking method. The episode closes with listener mail from Michelle Marianni about a frightening cave tour in Belize.

segments.title: Opening banter and fracking intro
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the topic and the F word, then discuss peak oil, US energy independence, natural gas hype, and the public's limited awareness of fracking.

segments.title: What fracking is and where it happens
segments.summary: Fracking is a technique for reaching deep shale deposits of oil and gas. Shale is a porous rock that traps gas and oil under pressure. The Marcellus Shale spans Pennsylvania, Ohio, New York, Virginia, Maryland and West Virginia, and New York's fracking ban and local municipal actions are mentioned, along with divided landowner opinions.

segments.title: Drilling, casing and perforating the well
segments.summary: A vertical well turns horizontal at a kickoff point, often 6,000 to 13,000 feet down. Steel casing is set and cemented, then explosive charges perforate the casing and surrounding rock.

segments.title: Pumping water, sand and chemicals
segments.summary: High-pressure water mixed with sand and chemicals is pumped down to crack the shale. Sand props the cracks open, and the fluid flows back up as wastewater. The whole process takes about four months and wells can produce for decades. Diesel use in fluid continues despite an EPA memorandum of agreement, with 32 million gallons injected between 2005 and 2009.

segments.title: Pro-fracking arguments
segments.summary: Supporters point to efficient horizontal wells that limit surface footprint, job creation and tax revenue (17,600 jobs and $100 million for New York), reduced dependence on foreign oil, and natural gas burning more cleanly than coal. Critics note truck traffic, about 200 trucks per million gallons, and methane leaks.

segments.title: Gasland, Truth Land and water contamination
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Gasland documentary's flaming tap water scene, which officials attributed to natural methane rather than fracking, and the pro-industry Truth Land film, which did not disclose its oil industry funding. They explain that deep shale drilling should not reach aquifers if wells are cased correctly, while shallow coal bed methane is riskier. A listener noted problems usually come from faulty well construction.

segments.title: Wastewater, earthquakes and chemical disclosure
segments.summary: Fracking uses millions of gallons of water, with only about 15 to 50 percent recovered, and the wastewater is more toxic. Wastewater reuse, treatment, and disposal in other states are discussed. Earthquakes are linked to wastewater storage rather than fracking itself. Pennsylvania required chemical disclosure, but trade-secret loopholes remain. Listed additives include salt, lemon juice, detergent and guar-type thickeners, and the hosts discuss water stress in Texas and Pennsylvania.

segments.title: Halliburton loophole and industry-funded research
segments.summary: The 2005 Energy Policy Act exempted fracking from parts of the Safe Drinking Water Act, and the Clean Water Act definition of pollutant was changed. The hosts link this to Dick Cheney and a former Halliburton executive. They discuss the University of Texas study by Professor Groat that was retracted over undisclosed conflicts of interest, plus similar cases at Penn State and SUNY Buffalo, and a timeline of accidents including the Ohio methane explosion and Pennsylvania spills.

segments.title: Gel fracking and closing thoughts on natural gas
segments.summary: A propane gel fracking method is described: the propane turns to vapor and can be captured and reused, avoiding wastewater, and it has been used about a thousand times since 2008. The hosts conclude that natural gas is a good bridge fuel if regulated safely.

segments.title: Show promotion
segments.summary: Promotion for the hosts' Science Channel TV show and iTunes availability.

segments.title: Listener mail: caving in Belize
segments.summary: Michelle Marianni describes a frightening five-hour cave tour on her honeymoon in Belize, and the hosts respond. They then invite listener feedback on fracking operations.
